podcast.title: Leaked Sex Tape and Lawsuit (2005)
podcast.body: In 2005, a three-minute video of Fred Durst and his girlfriend was leaked online. Durst responded by suing 10 websites, seeking $70 million in damages. "2005, Fred Durst of Lempisket. Now, three minutes of him and his girlfriend was somehow leaked online."

podcast.title: Association with Nu Metal
podcast.body: Fred Durst was presented as a figure associated with Nu Metal, a genre that was dominant in North American new rock for a period after 1995. "yes, kids there was a time when we thought that Fred Durst was really pretty damn cool."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Warner Brothers' Rap Suggestion
podcast.body: Warner Brothers Records suggested that Mike Shinoda of Linkin Park should learn to rap in a style similar to Fred Durst. This was part of the label's efforts to influence Linkin Park's sound. "Mike should learn to wrap like Fred Durst."

xref.title: Confrontation with Fred Durst (Summer 2000)
xref.body: A concert in New York that summer saw Fred Durst of Limp Biscuit diss singer Scott Stapp, to which Stapp responded by challenging Durst to a boxing match. "Actually, the end of Creed involved a fight with Limp Biscuit. There was a concert in New York that summer, and Fred Durst discreed singer Scott Stapp, and Stapp responded by challenging Fred to a boxing match."

xref.title: Big Day Out Tragedy and Lawsuits (2001)
xref.body: As headliners at the Big Day Out festival in Sydney on January 21, 2001, Limp Bizkit's singer Fred Durst had pre-show concerns about inadequate security barriers, which he discussed multiple times with the promoter. Despite assurances, a massive crush occurred towards the stage during their first song, resulting in approximately 30 injuries and the death of 15-year-old Jessica Milicic, who died five days later from a heart attack caused by asphyxiation. An investigation closed in November 2002 without charges, but new security rules were implemented. Milicic's parents filed a civil suit against Limp Bizkit in November 2004, and the band was also sued by their own insurance company over legal fees, leading to speculation that these events contributed to their subsequent quiet period. "So, is it any wonder we haven't heard anything from Limpbiscat since then?"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Jessica Michalik's Death at Big Day Out (2001)
xref.body: At the Big Day Out Festival in Australia in 2001, 16-year-old Jessica Michalik was crushed in the mosh pit during Limp Bizkit's performance, dying five days later from a heart attack related to asphyxiation. The coroner criticized singer Fred Durst for "alarming and inflammatory comments" made as EMS tried to rescue Michalik. "16-year-old Jessica Malachik was crushed in the pit and died of a heart attack related to a sixiation five days later."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Public Disfavor & Internal Issues (Mid-2005)
xref.body: By mid-2005, Limp Biscuit, and Fred Durst in particular, had "worn out their welcome with the public" as their sound and approach had gone "out of style." This period was also marked by internal problems. "But by the middle of 2005, Limp Biscuit in general and Fred Durst in particular had worn out their welcome with the public."

xref.title: Reunion Announcement (February 11, 2009)
xref.body: On this date, Fred Durst posted a message on Twitter – "1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight" – signaling the band's official return. "And on February 11th of 2009, those who were following Fred on Twitter... got this message. 1am Pacific time. Limp Biscuit.com tonight."

xref.title: Assorted Controversial Actions
xref.body: Al Jourgensen has a long history of controversial and confrontational behaviors, including stealing drugs from Courtney Love, physically assaulting R. Kelly for an action that distressed Jourgensen's daughter, and attacking Metallica with vegetables. He also insisted that Limp Bizkit frontman Fred Durst wear nothing but a cowboy hat during a vocal session he produced, blew up Ministry's tour bus with a large firework purchased from a homeless person, and was ejected from the Grammy Awards for screaming at Beyoncé. "Al Jorgensen stole drugs from Courtney Love. He punched out our kelly for doing something that freaked out his daughter. He attacked Metallica with some vegetables."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Band's Stand Against Label Interference
xref.body: In an unusual move for a new band, Linkin Park directly met with Warner Brothers executives and firmly rejected various label suggestions, including demands to remove rapping, change Mike Shinoda's rap style to mimic Fred Durst, bring in a reggae vocalist named Matt Lyons, or introduce gimmicks for DJ Joe Hahn like wearing a cowboy hat and lab coat. They also refused to change their logo, which some at the label found "too Asian." "And the meeting was risky because new bands just don't show up in the boardrooms of major record labels and start dictating terms for how they were to be marketed and how their fan club should be treated."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Discovery by Korn's Fieldy
xref.body: After Korn's encounter with Fred Durst, Durst strategically sent a Limp Bizkit demo tape to Fieldy, a member of Korn. Fieldy was impressed by the demo and subsequently passed it on to Korn's management and the emerging nu-metal producer Ross Robinson. This crucial step paved the way for Limp Bizkit's major label deal. "When Corn got home, Fieldy found a limp biscuit demo in his mailbox."

xref.title: Fred Durst's Career as Interscope Records Executive
xref.body: Following his success with Limp Bizkit, Fred Durst transitioned into a significant role as a major executive at Interscope Records. This career path was a direct result of the opportunities that arose from his initial connection with Korn. "Fred has since become a major executive at Interscope Records."

xref.title: Fred Durst's Role in Crowd Incitement
xref.body: Limp Bizkit's vocalist, Fred Durst, was specifically cited for intensely riling up the crowd, contributing to an atmosphere where a negative incident, such as the fatal crowd crush at Big Day Out, was almost inevitable. Although initial lawsuits were dismissed, an insurance company later sued the band in 2005, arguing that Durst had incited the crowd to rush the stage. "At the same time, Lent Biscuit, vocalist Fred Durst especially, riled up the crowd so much that something bad was almost an inevitability."
